stages.name: Demand and price elasticity
stages.title: Demand and price elasticity
stages.sub: How diminishing satisfaction shapes the demand curve, and how to tell a slide from a shift and measure sensitivity to price.

steps.q: You eat a first slice of pizza and love it. The fourth slice tastes fine but adds much less enjoyment. Would you pay as much for that fourth slice as the first?
steps.hint: Think about how much extra satisfaction each further slice actually gives you.
steps.pre: Because each extra unit gives less satisfaction, buyers will only buy more if price falls. This is diminishing marginal utility shaping

steps.q: You want to plot how many pizzas people buy at £20, at £10 and at £5. What do you need on the two axes to draw this?
steps.right: Price on one axis, quantity on the other
steps.wrong: Income on one axis, satisfaction on the other
steps.hint: Demand links a price to a quantity bought at that price.

steps.q: Pizza's price falls, so you slide down along the same demand curve you drew. Now instead imagine your income rises, so at every price you now want more pizza. Does that fit on the same curve, or does the whole curve have to move?
steps.right: The whole curve has to move
steps.wrong: It still fits on the same curve
steps.hint: A price change moves you along a fixed curve. Can an income change be shown that way too?

steps.q: Suppose more people suddenly prefer pizza to burgers, with pizza's own price unchanged. Is this a slide along the curve or a shift of it, and what caused it?
steps.right: A shift, caused by something other than pizza's own price
steps.wrong: A slide, caused by pizza's own price falling
steps.hint: Price itself did not move here, so what kind of change is this?

steps.right: No, rail demand reacts far more
steps.wrong: Yes, a 10% rise affects both the same
